items.explanation: His father Daedalus made the wings to escape Crete and warned him to fly neither too low nor too high. Phaethon also fell from the sky, after losing control of the Sun's chariot.
items.stem: In Greek myth, who flew too close to the Sun on wings of feathers and wax?

items.explanation: Poe published the poem in 1845 and it made him famous. The raven perches on a bust of Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom, above the narrator's door.
items.stem: Which poet wrote 'The Raven', in which a bird answers every question with 'Nevermore'?

items.explanation: Shylock is the moneylender. Antonio, the merchant, borrows from him on behalf of his friend Bassanio and pledges a pound of his own flesh as security.
items.stem: In Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice, who is the merchant of the title?

items.explanation: The 1939 film made them ruby slippers to show off its Technicolor. In the book they are silver and belonged to the Wicked Witch of the East.
items.stem: In L. Frank Baum's 1900 novel The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, what colour are Dorothy's magic shoes?

items.explanation: Daphne du Maurier never gives her narrator a first name. She is simply the second Mrs de Winter, overshadowed by Rebecca, her husband's first wife.
items.stem: Which novel begins 'Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again'?

items.explanation: Babylonian scribes were copying Gilgamesh about a thousand years before the Iliad took shape. Its flood story, in which birds are sent out to find dry land, echoes Noah's.
items.stem: Which came first?

items.explanation: His pen name means 'banana plant', after one that a student gave him for his hut. The frog poem, from 1686, has 17 sound units in Japanese, in lines of five, seven and five.
items.stem: Which Japanese poet wrote the famous haiku about a frog jumping into an old pond?

items.explanation: Many actors avoid saying the play's name inside a theatre, calling it 'the Scottish play' to dodge its supposed curse.
items.stem: Which Shakespeare play features three witches chanting 'Double, double toil and trouble'?

items.explanation: Lindgren first told Pippi stories to her daughter Karin, who invented the name while ill in bed. The first book came out in Sweden in 1945.
items.stem: Which author created Pippi Longstocking, the girl strong enough to lift a horse?

items.explanation: Kafka grew up in a German-speaking Jewish family in Prague, then part of Austria-Hungary. He also spoke Czech fluently, but wrote The Trial and The Metamorphosis in German.
items.stem: Franz Kafka spent most of his life in Prague. In which language did he write?

items.explanation: Charles Dickens published it in 1859. Set during the French Revolution, it moves between London and Paris, the two cities of the title.
items.stem: Which novel opens with 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times'?

items.explanation: The druid Getafix brews it, with mistletoe among the ingredients. Obelix needs none, because he fell into the cauldron as a baby and the effect stayed.
items.stem: In the Asterix comics, what gives the Gauls their superhuman strength?

items.explanation: Holmes says 'Elementary' and 'my dear Watson', but never together in Conan Doyle's 60 stories. The joined-up line spread later through films and other writers.
items.stem: In Arthur Conan Doyle's stories, Sherlock Holmes says 'Elementary, my dear Watson'.

items.explanation: The Iliad never mentions the heel. The story of his mother dipping him in the River Styx, holding him by one heel, first appears in Roman-era poetry.
items.stem: Which Greek hero could be wounded only at his heel?

items.explanation: A walk by a lake in April 1802 inspired it. His sister Dorothy described the same daffodils in her journal, which he drew on.
items.learnMore: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
items.stem: In William Wordsworth's 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud', which flowers does the poet see?

items.explanation: Hamlet says 'I knew him, Horatio', not the often-quoted 'I knew him well'. Feste, Touchstone and Trinculo are fools in other Shakespeare plays.
items.stem: In Hamlet, what is the name of the dead jester whose skull Hamlet holds?

items.explanation: Chinua Achebe, a tempting guess, never won a Nobel Prize. Soyinka is chiefly a playwright, and his plays include Death and the King's Horseman.
items.stem: Which Nigerian writer was awarded the 1986 Nobel Prize in Literature?

items.explanation: Snoopy made the line famous again by typing it at the start of his novels in Peanuts, and a contest for deliberately dreadful opening sentences was named after Bulwer-Lytton.
items.learnMore: It was a dark and stormy night
items.stem: Which writer opened his 1830 novel Paul Clifford with 'It was a dark and stormy night'?

items.explanation: Superman debuted in Action Comics in 1938. Spider-Man, created by Stan Lee and Steve Ditko, followed 24 years later in Amazing Fantasy.
items.stem: Which superhero appeared first?

items.explanation: Odysseus had been away for 20 years. Old and neglected, Argos wags his tail and drops his ears at the sight of his master, then dies.
items.stem: In the Odyssey, what is the name of the old dog who recognizes Odysseus when he comes home in disguise?

items.explanation: Aldous Huxley's novel came out 17 years before George Orwell's. Years earlier, Huxley had briefly taught French at Eton, where one of his pupils was Eric Blair, the future Orwell.
items.stem: Which was published first?

items.explanation: The prize honoured poems he had rendered into English himself, such as Gitanjali. Tagore also wrote the songs that became the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.
items.stem: In 1913, who became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature?

items.explanation: Iago even warns Othello against jealousy, 'the green-eyed monster', while stoking it. Cassio is the officer Iago falsely pairs with Desdemona.
items.stem: In Shakespeare's Othello, which character tricks Othello into believing his wife is unfaithful?

items.explanation: Murasaki Shikibu, a lady at Japan's imperial court, wrote Genji about six centuries before Cervantes. Each book is often called the first novel, in different senses.
items.stem: Which was written first?

items.explanation: Tezuka also qualified as a medical doctor. His robot boy, known in Japan as Mighty Atom, became a TV cartoon series in 1963.
items.stem: Which Japanese artist, often called 'the god of manga', created Astro Boy?

items.explanation: Stoker's Count is weaker by day but strolls through London in daylight. Vampires dying in sunlight came later, popularized by the 1922 film Nosferatu.
items.stem: In Bram Stoker's novel Dracula, the Count can walk about in daylight.

items.explanation: Coleridge said the poem came to him in a dream, and the rest slipped away during the visit. Writers still call an unwelcome interrupter 'a person from Porlock'.
items.stem: Which Coleridge poem did he say was cut short when 'a person on business from Porlock' interrupted him?

items.explanation: 'Wherefore' means 'why'. Juliet is asking why the boy she loves must be Romeo, a Montague, from the family at war with her own.
items.stem: When Juliet says 'wherefore art thou Romeo', she is asking where Romeo is.

items.explanation: The Grimm brothers published Children's and Household Tales in 1812. Andersen's first booklet followed in 1835, and unlike the Grimms, who collected folk tales, he invented most of his own.
items.stem: Which came first?
options: The first Grimm fairy tale book
The first Andersen fairy tale book

items.explanation: It builds to Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812. Tolstoy knew war first-hand: he served as an artillery officer in the Crimean War, at Sevastopol.
items.stem: Leo Tolstoy's War and Peace is set mainly during which conflict?

items.explanation: The other names belong to Austen heroes too: Frederick Wentworth in Persuasion, Edward Ferrars in Sense and Sensibility and George Knightley in Emma.
items.stem: What is Mr Darcy's full name in Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice?

items.explanation: She grew up in Tehran during the 1979 revolution and the war with Iraq. The title is the ancient Persian capital whose ruins stand near Shiraz.
items.stem: Marjane Satrapi's graphic memoir Persepolis tells of her childhood in which country?

items.explanation: The stories began with the Akan people of Ghana and crossed to the Caribbean with enslaved Africans. Tortoise and Hare are tricksters in other African traditions.
items.stem: Anansi, the trickster of many West African and Caribbean folk tales, usually takes the form of which creature?

items.explanation: Crusoe names him after the day of the week he saved his life. Defoe's 1719 novel was first presented as Crusoe's own true account, 'written by himself'.
items.stem: In Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe, what does Crusoe name the man he rescues?

items.explanation: Dante's deepest circle is Cocytus, a lake of ice. Satan is frozen chest-deep in it, and the beating of his huge wings makes the freezing wind that keeps it solid.
items.stem: In Dante's Inferno, what lies at the very bottom of Hell?

items.explanation: The first Globe burned down in 1613 when a stage cannon set its thatched roof alight during a performance of Henry VIII. A reconstruction opened near the site in 1997.
items.stem: Which London theatre, built in 1599, staged many of Shakespeare's plays?

items.explanation: In Andersen's 1837 tale the prince marries a princess. The mermaid dissolves into sea foam and rises as a spirit of the air, far from the ending of Disney's 1989 film.
items.stem: In Hans Christian Andersen's original story, the little mermaid marries the prince.

items.explanation: In 1849 Dostoevsky stood before a firing squad, until a last-minute reprieve from the Tsar sent him to a Siberian prison camp instead.
items.stem: Which Russian novelist wrote Crime and Punishment?

items.explanation: Dupin first appeared in 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue' in 1841. In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes sniffs that Dupin was 'a very inferior fellow'.
items.stem: Which detective appeared first in print?

items.explanation: Her creator, the psychologist William Moulton Marston, had worked on a blood-pressure test for lying that fed into the polygraph. She first appeared in 1941.
items.stem: Which superhero carries a golden Lasso of Truth?

items.explanation: Loki, usually male, turned himself into a mare to lure away the stallion of a giant building the walls of Asgard. The foal he later bore was Sleipnir.
items.stem: In Norse myth, who gave birth to Sleipnir, Odin's eight-legged horse?

items.explanation: Stevenson describes Hyde as small and young-looking, so Jekyll's clothes hang loose on him. Stage and film versions often turned Hyde into a hulking brute.
items.learnMore: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
items.stem: In Robert Louis Stevenson's story, Mr Hyde is smaller than Dr Jekyll.

items.explanation: Edward Lear made the form famous with A Book of Nonsense in 1846. Its shorter third and fourth lines rhyme with each other.
items.stem: Which comic verse form has five lines, with the first, second and fifth rhyming?

items.explanation: Kan'ami and his son Zeami shaped Noh in Japan in the late 1300s, two centuries before Shakespeare. A Noh stage traditionally has a pine tree painted on its back wall.
items.stem: Which came first?

items.explanation: Antoine Galland, who heard the tale from the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab, set it in a city in China. The wicked sorcerer, by contrast, comes from the Maghreb, in north-west Africa.
items.stem: In the oldest known version of the story, Aladdin lives in which country?

items.explanation: Charles M. Schulz drew all of the nearly 18,000 Peanuts strips himself, from 1950 to 2000. Snoopy began as an ordinary four-legged dog and only later walked on two legs.
items.stem: In the Peanuts comic strip, what breed of dog is Snoopy?

items.explanation: Born Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski to Polish parents in 1857, he learned French next and took up English only in his twenties, as a merchant seaman.
items.stem: What was the first language of Joseph Conrad, author of Heart of Darkness?

items.explanation: Mark Antony speaks it at Caesar's funeral. He claims he has come to bury Caesar, not to praise him, then turns the crowd against Brutus and the other conspirators.
items.learnMore: Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears
items.stem: Which Shakespeare play contains the line 'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears'?

items.explanation: Sun Wukong guards the monk Tang Sanzang on a journey to India. The monk is based on Xuanzang, a real 7th-century pilgrim who brought Buddhist scriptures back to China.
items.stem: The Monkey King, Sun Wukong, is a hero of which classic Chinese novel?

items.explanation: Alice follows him down the rabbit hole. Lewis Carroll first told the story to Alice Liddell and her sisters on a boat trip near Oxford in July 1862.
items.stem: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, which character frets about being late and checks his pocket watch?

items.explanation: Batman first appeared in Detective Comics in 1939. That title gave the publisher its name: the DC in DC Comics stands for Detective Comics.
items.stem: Which superhero's secret identity is Bruce Wayne?

items.explanation: In some tellings, Arthur draws a different sword from a stone and later receives Excalibur from the Lady of the Lake. Durendal, Joyeuse and Tizona belonged to Roland, Charlemagne and El Cid.
items.stem: In Arthurian legend, what is the name of King Arthur's sword?

items.explanation: Orwell's 1945 fable mirrors the Russian Revolution and what followed: the pigs Napoleon and Snowball stand for Stalin and Trotsky.
items.stem: In George Orwell's Animal Farm, which animals end up ruling the farm?

items.explanation: The Swedish Academy cited him 'for having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition'. He skipped the ceremony and sent his lecture as a recording months later.
items.stem: Which singer-songwriter was awarded the 2016 Nobel Prize in Literature?

items.explanation: Beckett had settled in Paris and wrote it as En attendant Godot, first staged there in 1953. He then made the English version himself.
items.stem: Irish-born Samuel Beckett first wrote Waiting for Godot in which language?

items.explanation: Potter first told the Peter Rabbit story in an illustrated letter to a sick child in 1893. Earnings from her books helped her buy Lake District farms, which she left to the National Trust.
items.stem: Which author and illustrator created Peter Rabbit?

items.explanation: Dumas based him on a real officer, Charles de Batz de Castelmore d'Artagnan, who served Louis XIV. The three of the title are Athos, Porthos and Aramis.
items.stem: In Alexandre Dumas's The Three Musketeers, what is the name of the young Gascon who joins them?

items.explanation: In Ovid's telling, the wine god Bacchus granted the wish. When even his food turned to metal, Midas washed the gift away in the river Pactolus, whose sands then glittered with gold.
items.stem: In Greek myth, King Midas was granted a wish that turned everything he touched into what?

items.explanation: Ariadne, daughter of King Minos, gave Theseus a ball of thread to find his way out. The Minotaur, half man and half bull, was her half-brother.
items.stem: Which hero of Greek myth killed the Minotaur in the Labyrinth on Crete?

items.explanation: Perseus cut off her head while watching her reflection in a polished shield, so he never met her gaze. The winged horse Pegasus sprang from her body.
items.stem: In Greek myth, anyone who looked at the Gorgon Medusa was turned into what?

items.explanation: Herodotus recorded an Egyptian story that a phoenix visited Heliopolis once every 500 years, but admitted he had seen one only in paintings.
items.stem: Which mythical bird is said to be reborn from its own ashes?

items.explanation: Hamelin is a real town in Germany. When the town refused to pay him, the piper led its children away too, a story Robert Browning retold in an 1842 poem.
items.stem: In the legend of the Pied Piper of Hamelin, which pests does the piper lead out of the town?

items.explanation: Little is known about Aesop himself. Ancient writers, including Herodotus, said he was an enslaved man on the Greek island of Samos in the 500s BC.
items.stem: Which ancient storyteller is credited with the fable of the tortoise and the hare?

items.explanation: In Māori tradition, New Zealand's North Island is Te Ika-a-Māui, 'the fish of Māui', and his hook was carved from his grandmother's jawbone.
items.stem: In Polynesian myth, what did the demigod Māui use to haul islands up from the sea?

items.explanation: Sundiata Keita founded the empire in the 13th century. Griots, West Africa's hereditary storytellers and musicians, have passed the epic down by word of mouth for centuries.
items.stem: The Epic of Sundiata, kept alive by griots, tells of the founder of which West African empire?

items.explanation: Its branches and roots join the nine worlds. In the Prose Edda an eagle perches at the top, a dragon gnaws a root, and a squirrel carries insults between them.
items.stem: In Norse myth, what is Yggdrasil?

items.explanation: Virgil modelled the Aeneid on Homer about seven centuries later. Dying in 19 BC with the poem unfinished, he asked for it to be burned, but Emperor Augustus refused.
items.stem: Which epic was composed first?

items.explanation: The Iliad covers a few weeks in the war's tenth year and ends with Hector's funeral, before the city falls. The horse is recalled in the Odyssey and told in full in Virgil's Aeneid.
items.stem: Homer's Iliad tells the story of the wooden Trojan Horse.

items.explanation: Petrarch's sonnets divide into eight lines and six. Shakespeare's run as three quatrains of four lines and end with a rhyming couplet that often turns the argument.
items.stem: How many lines does a traditional sonnet have?

items.explanation: The owl and the cat dine on mince and slices of quince, eaten with a 'runcible spoon'. Lear made up the word runcible, and nobody knows exactly what he meant by it.
items.stem: Which poet wrote 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat', in which the pair go to sea in a pea-green boat?

items.explanation: Khayyam was also a mathematician and astronomer who helped reform the Persian calendar. FitzGerald's loose English version of the quatrains appeared in 1859.
items.stem: The Rubaiyat, made famous in English by Edward FitzGerald, is credited to which Persian poet?

items.explanation: Moonlight before his bed looks like frost on the ground; he raises his head to the bright Moon, then lowers it, thinking of home. Generations of Chinese children have learned it by heart.
items.stem: In Li Bai's poem 'Quiet Night Thought', what does the poet gaze up at before thinking of home?

items.explanation: Gabriela Mistral was the pen name of Lucila Godoy Alcayaga, a schoolteacher. Pablo Neruda followed her as Chile's second literature laureate, in 1971.
items.stem: Which Chilean poet became the first Latin American writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1945?

items.explanation: She wrote nearly 1,800 poems, mostly kept private. After her death in 1886, her sister Lavinia found them, and the first collection appeared in 1890.
items.stem: Fewer than a dozen of Emily Dickinson's poems were published during her lifetime.

items.explanation: The feud between the Capulets and Romeo's family, the Montagues, drives the play. Shakespeare took the story from Arthur Brooke's 1562 poem about Romeus and Juliet.
items.stem: In Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, what is Juliet's family name?

items.explanation: The bear chases Antigonus off the stage in Act 3. Scholars have long debated whether early performances used a real bear or an actor in a costume.
items.stem: Which Shakespeare play contains the famous stage direction 'Exit, pursued by a bear'?

items.explanation: Prospero's daughter Miranda, who has seen almost no other people, greets a group of strangers with 'O brave new world, that has such people in't'. Huxley borrowed it with heavy irony.
items.stem: Aldous Huxley took the title Brave New World from a line in which Shakespeare play?

items.explanation: His nurse, Miss Prism, absent-mindedly put him in the bag and the manuscript of her three-volume novel in his baby carriage. The bag ended up at Victoria station.
items.stem: In Oscar Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest, where was Jack Worthing found as a baby?

items.explanation: Cervantes called Lope de Vega a 'monster of nature' for his output. He claimed to have written about 1,500 plays, and several hundred survive, against roughly 38 by Shakespeare.
items.stem: Which playwright has more surviving plays?

items.explanation: Hagrid buys the owl as a present for Harry's 11th birthday in the first book. Errol and Pigwidgeon are Weasley family owls, and Fawkes belongs to Dumbledore.
items.stem: In the Harry Potter books, what is the name of Harry's owl?

items.explanation: Dahl drew on his schooldays at Repton, where the chocolate maker Cadbury sent boxes of new bars for pupils to taste and rate.
items.stem: In Roald Dahl's Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, who works in Willy Wonka's factory?

items.explanation: Strictly, a butterfly forms a chrysalis, not the cocoon the book describes. The pages have holes punched through them wherever the caterpillar has eaten.
items.stem: At the end of Eric Carle's The Very Hungry Caterpillar, what does the caterpillar become?

items.explanation: The giant's chant is older than the printed tale: in King Lear, written around 1606, Shakespeare's Edgar says 'Fie, foh, and fum, I smell the blood of a British man.'
items.stem: Which fairy-tale hero climbs a beanstalk to a giant's castle in the clouds?

items.explanation: In Robert Southey's 1837 telling, the intruder is a bad-tempered old woman. A golden-haired girl took her place in later versions.
items.stem: In the story of Goldilocks and the Three Bears, whose porridge is just right?

items.explanation: Collodi's puppet first appeared as a magazine serial in 1881. In a famous scene his nose grows so long that he cannot get through the door, and woodpeckers peck it back to size.
items.stem: In Carlo Collodi's story, what happens to Pinocchio's nose when he tells a lie?

items.explanation: On Earth a fox tells him that what is essential is invisible to the eye. Saint-Exupéry, a pilot, drew on his own 1935 crash in the Sahara for the narrator's story.
items.stem: In Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's The Little Prince, what does the prince love on his tiny home planet?

items.explanation: Sewell wrote it to encourage kindness to working horses. Its title page called it the autobiography of a horse, 'translated from the original equine'.
items.stem: Anna Sewell's only novel, published in 1877, is narrated by a horse. What is it called?

items.explanation: His publisher, Bennett Cerf, bet him that he could not write a book with only 50 distinct words. Seuss won the bet with the 1960 book.
items.stem: Dr. Seuss wrote Green Eggs and Ham using just 50 different words.

items.explanation: In the Grimms' tale, the prince's servants stumble while carrying her glass coffin, and the jolt dislodges the poisoned apple from her throat. The kiss was made famous by Disney's film.
items.stem: In the Brothers Grimm's Snow White, a prince's kiss breaks the spell and wakes her.

items.explanation: Perrault's 1697 tale has the fairy godmother, the pumpkin coach and the glass slipper. In the Grimms' Aschenputtel, a hazel tree on her mother's grave and helpful birds grant her wishes.
items.stem: Which version of Cinderella was published first?

items.explanation: Ali Baba first appeared in print in Antoine Galland's French translation of the Arabian Nights, in the early 1700s; no older Arabic text of the tale is known.
items.learnMore: Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves
items.stem: In the tale of Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves, which words open the robbers' cave?

items.explanation: Borges became director of Argentina's National Library in 1955, when he was almost blind. In a poem he marvelled that God had given him books and the night at once.
items.stem: Which Argentine writer imagined 'The Library of Babel', a vast library holding every possible book?

items.explanation: Norwegian Wood (1987) takes its title from a Beatles song. Before writing full time, Murakami ran a jazz bar in Tokyo.
items.stem: Which Japanese author wrote the novels Norwegian Wood and Kafka on the Shore?

items.explanation: Eco was a professor of semiotics, the study of signs. His monk detective, William of Baskerville, is a nod to Sherlock Holmes and The Hound of the Baskervilles.
items.stem: Which Italian author wrote The Name of the Rose, a murder mystery set in a medieval monastery?

items.explanation: Gannibal was brought to Russia as a boy and became Peter the Great's godson. Pushkin began a historical novel about him but never finished it.
items.stem: Which Russian poet's great-grandfather, Abram Gannibal, was born in Africa and rose to become a general?

items.explanation: The line comes from Yeats's poem 'The Second Coming', written in 1919: 'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold.' Achebe's 1958 novel follows an Igbo leader as colonial rule arrives.
items.stem: Chinua Achebe took the title Things Fall Apart from a poem by which writer?

items.explanation: In its longest form the Mahabharata has over 100,000 couplets, and it is often called the longest poem ever composed. War and Peace is about a third of its length.
items.stem: Which is longer, by number of words?

items.explanation: Melville named the ship after the Pequot people of New England. Its first mate, Starbuck, gave his name to a coffee chain whose founders had first considered calling it Pequod.
items.stem: In Herman Melville's Moby-Dick, what is the name of Captain Ahab's whaling ship?

items.explanation: The 1726 satire gave English the word 'Lilliputian', meaning very small. On his next voyage, to Brobdingnag, Gulliver is the tiny one among giants.
items.stem: In Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels, what is the land of tiny people called?

items.explanation: Nemo is Latin for 'no one'. In a later novel, The Mysterious Island, the captain is revealed to be Prince Dakkar, the son of an Indian raja.
items.stem: Which author created Captain Nemo and his submarine, the Nautilus?

items.explanation: Mark Twain was the pen name of Samuel Clemens. It comes from a riverboat call meaning two fathoms deep, about 3.7 m (12 feet), safe water for a steamboat.
items.stem: Which author wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer?

items.explanation: The parrot is named after the pirate who buried the treasure, and it screeches 'Pieces of eight'. Silver reckons the bird may be 200 years old.
items.stem: In Treasure Island, what is the name of Long John Silver's parrot?

items.explanation: Victor Hugo set his novel in 1482 but published it in 1831, 13 years after Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. Its French title is simply Notre-Dame de Paris.
items.stem: Which novel was published first?

items.explanation: Defoe placed the island off the mouth of the Orinoco, within sight of Trinidad. The real castaway Alexander Selkirk was marooned in the Pacific, on an island renamed Robinson Crusoe Island in 1966.
items.stem: In Defoe's novel, Robinson Crusoe is shipwrecked on an island in the Pacific Ocean.

items.explanation: Leo Tolstoy published it in instalments from 1875 to 1877. Scientists later named the 'Anna Karenina principle' after the opening: success needs many things to go right, failure only one.
items.stem: Which novel opens by saying that happy families are all alike, but each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way?

items.explanation: The sentence ends 'that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.' Austen's first title for the book was First Impressions.
items.stem: Which novel opens with the words 'It is a truth universally acknowledged'?

items.explanation: George Orwell published it in 1949. Its hero, Winston Smith, works at the Ministry of Truth, rewriting old newspaper reports so the record always matches the Party's line.
items.stem: Which novel opens on 'a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen'?

items.explanation: Arthur Conan Doyle created Moriarty for 'The Final Problem' (1893) so the two could plunge together over the Reichenbach Falls. Readers' dismay helped bring Holmes back in 1903.
items.stem: Which criminal mastermind does Sherlock Holmes call 'the Napoleon of crime'?

items.explanation: Bilbo and Frodo share a birthday, 22 September, and in Tolkien's Shire hobbits give presents to other people on their own birthdays.
items.stem: In The Lord of the Rings, which hobbit inherits the One Ring from his cousin Bilbo?

items.explanation: Holmes first appeared in A Study in Scarlet in 1887, nearly a decade before Dracula. Conan Doyle, who knew Stoker, wrote to praise the vampire novel.
items.stem: Which came first?

items.explanation: In Hergé's original French he is called Milou. He is a white wire fox terrier, while Dogmatix is Obelix's little dog in the Asterix books.
items.stem: In the English translations of The Adventures of Tintin, what is Tintin's dog called?

items.explanation: Jim Davis, who grew up on a farm with about 25 cats, launched the strip in 1978 and named its hero after his grandfather, James Garfield Davis.
items.stem: Which comic-strip cat loves lasagne and hates Mondays?

items.explanation: Watterson named the pair after the theologian John Calvin and the philosopher Thomas Hobbes. He ended the strip in 1995 and refused to license the characters for merchandise.
items.stem: Which cartoonist created the comic strip Calvin and Hobbes, about a boy and his toy tiger?

items.explanation: Eiichiro Oda began the series in 1997 in the magazine Weekly Shōnen Jump. Luffy's stretchy body comes from eating a Devil Fruit, which also leaves him unable to swim.
items.stem: Monkey D. Luffy, a pirate whose body stretches like rubber, is the hero of which manga?

items.explanation: Tintin first appeared in 1929 in Le Petit Vingtième, a Belgian newspaper's children's supplement. Asterix arrived 30 years later, in 1959, in the first issue of the French magazine Pilote.
items.stem: Which comic hero appeared first?
